lessons.title: Common Banana Pests: Weevils, Nematodes, Aphids
lessons.body:
Banana weevils (Cosmopolites sordidus) are the most destructive insect pests in African banana farms. The adult weevil is black, about 1 cm long, and hides in leaf litter and soil around the base of the plant. Females lay eggs in small holes they chew in the corm. The larvae tunnel inside the corm, causing stunting, poor bunch filling, and snapping of the pseudostem. You can detect weevils by cutting a piece of pseudostem and placing it on the ground; weevils will hide inside within 24 hours. Control: use clean planting material, remove old corms and crop residues, apply neem cake (200 g per mat) or entomopathogenic nematodes. Chemical control: apply imidacloprid or bifenthrin at planting and every 3 months.

Nematodes (Radopholus similis, Pratylenchus goodeyi) are microscopic roundworms that feed on roots, causing root death, toppling, and reduced yields. They enter through root tips and create lesions. To check, dig up roots and look for dark, necrotic spots. In Africa, the burrowing nematode (R. similis) is common in Uganda, Kenya, and Tanzania. Control: plant clean tissue-culture plantlets, apply nematicides like fenamiphos (5 g per mat) or organic amendments such as poultry manure (5 kg per mat) and marigold intercropping. Crop rotation with maize or beans for 6 months reduces populations.

Aphids (Pentalonia nigronervosa) are small, brown to black, and cluster on young leaves and pseudostems. They suck sap and excrete honeydew, which attracts ants. More importantly, aphids transmit Banana Bunchy Top Virus (BBTV) and Banana Mosaic Virus. In Africa, BBTV is a major threat in Malawi, Uganda, and Rwanda. Control: monitor weekly, remove and destroy infected plants, encourage natural predators like ladybirds and lacewings, and apply insecticidal soap (10 ml per litre of water) or imidacloprid. Avoid excessive nitrogen fertiliser, which promotes aphid outbreaks. Always use certified virus-free planting material.

lessons.title: Major Fungal Diseases: Panama Disease, Sigatoka
lessons.body:
Panama disease (Fusarium wilt) is caused by the soil fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense. It enters through roots, blocks water-conducting vessels, and causes yellowing of older leaves, splitting of the pseudostem, and eventual plant death. The fungus survives in soil for decades. In Africa, Tropical Race 4 (TR4) has devastated Cavendish bananas in Mozambique and is spreading. There is no chemical cure. Control: use resistant varieties (e.g., FHIA hybrids), plant in clean soil, and quarantine affected areas. If you suspect Panama disease, uproot and burn the entire mat, then treat the hole with lime (1 kg per hole) and leave fallow for 6 months. Avoid moving soil or suckers from infected fields.

Black Sigatoka (Mycosphaerella fijiensis) is the most serious leaf disease in African banana farms. It causes dark streaks on leaves that enlarge into black spots, reducing photosynthesis and yield by 30-50%. It spreads by wind and rain. In Uganda, unmanaged Sigatoka can reduce bunch weight from 20 kg to 10 kg. Control: remove infected leaves weekly (deleafing), improve drainage, and apply fungicides. A common programme: mancozeb (2 kg/ha) every 2 weeks, alternating with propiconazole (0.5 L/ha) every 4 weeks. For organic farms, use copper hydroxide (2 kg/ha) every 10 days. Resistant varieties like FHIA-25 are available. Yellow Sigatoka (M. musicola) is less aggressive but still reduces yield; same control measures apply.

Prevention is key: plant in well-drained soil, space plants 3 m x 3 m for air circulation, and avoid overhead irrigation. Remove old leaves and pseudostems after harvest. Keep records of disease outbreaks. If you see black streaks on leaves, act immediatelyâdo not wait for spots to form. For both diseases, sanitation and resistant varieties are your best long-term defence.

lessons.title: Viral Diseases: Bunchy Top, Mosaic
lessons.body:
Banana Bunchy Top Virus (BBTV) is the most devastating viral disease in Africa. It is transmitted by the banana aphid (Pentalonia nigronervosa). Symptoms: new leaves are narrow, upright, and bunched at the top, with dark green streaks on petioles and midribs. The plant produces no bunch. Once infected, there is no cure. In Malawi, BBTV reduced yields by 90% in some districts. Control: use virus-free tissue-culture plantlets, control aphids with imidacloprid (0.5 ml per litre) or insecticidal soap, and immediately uproot and burn infected plants. Do not compost them. Quarantine: do not move suckers from infected areas. Inspect your farm weekly for symptoms. If you find a plant with bunched leaves, remove it and all its suckers, then kill aphids on neighbouring plants.

Banana Mosaic Virus (BaMV) causes yellow streaks and mottling on leaves, stunting, and small bunches. It spreads through infected planting material and possibly by aphids. In East Africa, it is less common than BBTV but still reduces yield by 20-40%. Control: same as BBTVâuse clean planting material, remove infected plants, and control aphids. There is no chemical cure for viruses. The best strategy is prevention: buy certified plantlets from reputable tissue-culture labs (e.g., in Kenya, Uganda, or South Africa).

For both viruses, field hygiene is critical. Tools used on infected plants must be disinfected with 10% bleach solution or 70% alcohol. Wear gloves and wash hands after handling infected plants. Do not plant new bananas near old infected fields. If you intercrop, avoid hosts like tobacco, which can carry mosaic viruses. Train workers to recognise symptoms early. A single infected plant can spread the virus to your entire farm within a season. Report outbreaks to local extension officers. In some countries, government compensation is available for uprooted infected mats. Always keep a map of your farm and mark infected spots. After removing infected plants, leave the area fallow for 3 months before replanting with clean material.

lessons.title: Integrated Pest Management (IPM) Strategies
lessons.body:
Integrated Pest Management (IPM) means using a combination of methodsâcultural, biological, physical, and chemicalâto keep pests and diseases below damaging levels. For banana farming in Africa, IPM starts with prevention. Use clean, certified tissue-culture plantlets. Space plants 3 m x 3 m to allow airflow and reduce humidity. Plant cover crops like beans or sweet potatoes between rows to suppress weeds and improve soil. Rotate bananas with maize or cassava for 6 months if nematodes or Panama disease are present.

Monitor your farm weekly. Walk in a zigzag pattern and inspect 10 random plants per hectare. Look for weevil holes, aphid clusters, leaf streaks, and yellowing. Keep a notebook. Set action thresholds: for aphids, treat if you find 5 or more aphids per plant; for weevils, treat if 10% of plants show damage. Use pheromone traps for weevils (1 trap per 10 m x 10 m) and yellow sticky traps for aphids (10 traps per hectare).

Biological control: encourage natural enemies. Ladybirds, lacewings, and parasitic wasps attack aphids. Predatory mites and nematodes attack weevil larvae. Apply neem oil (5 ml per litre) or Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) for caterpillars. For nematodes, apply Paecilomyces lilacinus (a fungus) at 5 g per mat. These are safe for humans and beneficial insects.

Cultural practices: remove old leaves and pseudostems after harvest. Chop them and spread as mulch, but not near the baseâkeep 30 cm away to avoid weevil breeding. Destroy infected plants immediately. Use drip irrigation instead of overhead to keep leaves dry. Apply balanced fertiliser (e.g., NPK 17-17-17, 200 g per mat every 3 months) to keep plants strong. Avoid excess nitrogen, which attracts aphids.

Chemical control is a last resort. Rotate chemicals to prevent resistance. Use protective gear. Never spray during flowering or when bees are active. Record every spray. Combine all these methods for the best results. IPM reduces costs, protects the environment, and gives healthier bananas.

lessons.title: Biological and Chemical Control Methods
lessons.body:
Biological control uses living organisms to manage pests. For banana weevils, the entomopathogenic nematode Steinernema carpocapsae can be applied to the soil at 1 million nematodes per square metre. It seeks out weevil larvae and kills them within 48 hours. The fungus Beauveria bassiana (available as a wettable powder) can be sprayed on pseudostems and soil at 2 g per litre. For nematodes, the fungus Paecilomyces lilacinus (e.g., Bio-Nematon) is applied at 5 g per mat every 3 months. For aphids, release ladybirds (200 per hectare) or lacewing larvae (500 per hectare). You can also spray neem oil (10 ml per litre of water with 2 ml soap) every 7 days until aphids are gone. Bacillus thuringiensis var. kurstaki (Bt) controls leaf-eating caterpillars, not aphids or weevils.

Chemical control should be used only when pests exceed thresholds. Always read the label. For weevils, apply imidacloprid 200 SL at 0.5 ml per litre as a soil drench around the base, or bifenthrin 10 EC at 1 ml per litre. For nematodes, use fenamiphos 400 EC at 5 g per mat (but this is highly toxicâwear gloves and mask). For aphids, spray imidacloprid 200 SL at 0.25 ml per litre or insecticidal soap at 10 ml per litre. For fungal diseases, use mancozeb 80 WP at 2 kg per hectare every 14 days, alternating with propiconazole 250 EC at 0.5 L per hectare every 28 days. For organic farms, copper hydroxide at 2 kg per hectare every 10 days.

Safety: never mix chemicals without advice. Store in original containers away from children and animals. Spray early morning or late evening to protect bees. Wear long sleeves, gloves, boots, and a mask. Wash clothes separately after spraying. Do not eat, drink, or smoke while spraying. Observe pre-harvest intervals: for imidacloprid, wait 7 days; for mancozeb, 14 days. Dispose of empty containers by puncturing and burying, not burning. Keep records of all applications: date, product, rate, and pest. If you use biologicals, do not apply chemical fungicides within 3 days, as they kill beneficial fungi. Combine biological and chemical methods carefullyânever tank-mix unless the label says it is safe.

lessons.title: Sanitation and Quarantine Practices
lessons.body:
Sanitation is your first line of defence against banana pests and diseases. Start with clean tools. After pruning or harvesting each plant, dip your machete and knife in 10% bleach solution (1 part bleach to 9 parts water) or 70% alcohol for 30 seconds. This prevents spreading Fusarium, BBTV, and nematodes. Wear clean boots and clothes. If you walk through an infected field, wash boots with bleach before entering a healthy field. Do not move soil on tools or boots.

Remove and destroy infected plant material immediately. For BBTV or Panama disease, uproot the entire mat, including corms and suckers. Chop into pieces and burn, or bury deep (1 m) away from the farm. Do not compost. For Sigatoka, remove infected leaves weekly and burn them. Do not leave them on the ground. For weevils, remove old pseudostems and corms after harvest; chop and spread as mulch but keep 30 cm from plant bases. Clean up fallen fruits and flowers, which attract insects.

Quarantine means preventing the movement of pests and diseases into new areas. Never take suckers from a neighbour's farm unless you know it is disease-free. Buy only certified tissue-culture plantlets from reputable labs. If you must use suckers, treat them with hot water (52Â°C for 20 minutes) to kill nematodes and weevil eggs. After treatment, cool and plant immediately. Inspect all new planting material for symptoms: dark streaks, bunchy leaves, or root lesions. Reject any suspicious plants.

If you have an outbreak, quarantine your own farm. Do not sell or give away suckers from affected areas. Mark the boundary with signs. Restrict visitors. Report to local extension officers. In some African countries, quarantine regulations require you to notify authorities if you suspect Panama disease TR4 or BBTV. After removing infected plants, leave the area fallow for 3 months, then plant a non-host crop like maize or beans for one season before replanting bananas. Keep a farm map and record all sanitation activities. A clean farm is a productive farm.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Pest and Disease Management for Banana Farming in Africa

Banana and plantain (Musa spp.) are among the most important food and income security crops in sub-Saharan Africa, with the Great Lakes region (Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, DRC), Cameroon, Ghana, CÃ´te d'Ivoire, Kenya, and Tanzania accounting for the bulk of production. Smallholder productivity is typically 5â15 t/ha against a potential of 30â60 t/ha, and pests and diseases are the single largest yield gap driver â often causing 30â100% losses when unmanaged. For agribusinesses, this is not just an agronomic problem: it is a margin problem. Every tonne lost to weevils, nematodes, or Panama disease is a tonne not sold, not processed, and not reinvested. This reference module consolidates practical, field-tested management guidance for the AFRICA RISES skills pathway.

1. Common Banana Pests â Field Identification and Damage

Banana weevils (Cosmopolites sordidus) are the most economically damaging insect pest across African banana systems. Adult weevils lay eggs at the base of the pseudostem; larvae tunnel into the corm, weakening anchorage and blocking vascular flow. Symptoms include small oval entry holes, gum exudation, toppling, and reduced bunch weight. Nematodes â principally Radopholus similis, Pratylenchus goodeyi, and Helicotylenchus multicinctus â cause root necrosis, toppling, and yield losses of 30â60% in highland systems. Aphids (Pentalonia nigronervosa) are the primary vector of Banana Bunchy Top Virus and cause direct damage through sap feeding and honeydew-induced sooty mould.

Table 1: Key banana pests in Africa â damage and economic impact
Pest Damage symptom Typical yield loss Priority regions
Banana weevil (C. sordidus) Corm tunnelling, toppling, stunted bunches 30â80% Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Ghana
Burrowing nematode (R. similis) Root necrosis, toppling, poor uptake 30â60% Cameroon, CÃ´te d'Ivoire, DRC
Banana aphid (P. nigronervosa) Sooty mould, virus transmission Indirect, up to 100% via BBTV All banana-growing zones
Root-lesion nematode (P. goodeyi) Root decay, reduced bunch size 20â50% East African highlands

Source: IITA Banana Pest and Disease Fact Sheets; CABI Crop Protection Compendium.

2. Major Fungal Diseases

Panama disease (Fusarium wilt, Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense) is soil-borne and incurable once established. Tropical Race 4 (TR4) has been confirmed in Mozambique and is a serious threat to Cavendish export production. Symptoms include yellowing of older leaves from the margin inward, splitting of the pseudostem base, and vascular discolouration (brown-red streaks) in the corm. Black Sigatoka (Pseudocercospora fijiensis) causes dark streaks and leaf necrosis, reducing photosynthesis and bunch weight by 30â50%; it is the most costly disease to manage in commercial plantations. Yellow Sigatoka (P. musae) is less aggressive but still significant in humid zones.

Table 2: Fungal and viral disease management matrix
Disease Pathogen Key control measures Africa status
Panama disease (TR4) F. oxysporum f. sp. cubense Resistant cultivars, strict quarantine, no soil movement Confirmed in Mozambique; high risk elsewhere
Black Sigatoka P. fijiensis Deleafing, fungicide rotation, resistant hybrids Widespread in humid lowlands
Yellow Sigatoka P. musae Sanitation, canopy management Endemic in most zones
Banana Bunchy Top Virus BBTV (aphid-vectored) Roguing, aphid control, certified planting material Present in parts of East and Central Africa
Banana Mosaic Virus BSV / CMV complex Clean suckers, vector management Widespread but low severity

Source: FAO, Banana Fusarium Wilt Tropical Race 4 technical brief; IITA disease surveillance reports.

3. Integrated Pest Management (IPM) Strategies

IPM for banana is a sequenced decision framework, not a product list. Start with monitoring: weekly scouting using weevil traps (split pseudostem or pheromone traps), leaf disease scoring (Stover scale for Sigatoka), and root health assessment at 3â6 month intervals. Cultural controls include using certified disease-free tissue-culture plantlets or pared, hot-water-treated suckers; maintaining 2â3 m spacing for airflow; mulching to suppress nematodes; and removing old leaves and pseudostems. Biological controls include Beauveria bassiana and Metarhizium anisopliae for weevil suppression, and Trichoderma spp. for root disease complex management. Chemical controls are a last resort: approved nematicides and fungicides must be rotated by mode of action to prevent resistance, and applied only by trained personnel with full PPE.

4. Biological and Chemical Control Methods

Biological options are increasingly favoured in African markets, particularly for organic and export-certified supply chains. Beauveria bassiana applied to corm surfaces and pseudostem traps reduces weevil larval survival by 40â70% in field trials. Trichoderma harzianum and T. asperellum colonise root zones and suppress Fusarium and nematode populations. Chemical options â where registered â include imidacloprid or thiamethoxam for aphid control, and mancozeb, propiconazole, or azoxystrobin-based programmes for Sigatoka. Always check national registration (e.g., Kenya PCPB, Ghana EPA, Nigeria NAFDAC) before purchase; unregistered imports are a legal and market-access risk.

â  SAFETY WARNING â CHEMICAL HANDLING

Never apply pesticides without full personal protective equipment (gloves, mask, goggles, long sleeves, boots). Do not mix or apply near water sources, homes, or livestock. Observe pre-harvest intervals strictly â residues above maximum limits will cause rejection of export consignments. Store chemicals in locked, ventilated, labelled cabinets away from food and children. In case of poisoning, contact the nearest poison centre immediately and retain the product label. Unregistered or banned pesticides (e.g., paraquat, monocrotophos) must never be used on banana.

5. Sanitation and Quarantine Practices

Sanitation is the cheapest and most effective IPM pillar. Practices include: removing and destroying diseased pseudostems and corms (do not compost); debudding male flowers to reduce insect attraction; cleaning pruning tools with 10% bleach or 70% alcohol between plants; and maintaining footbaths and dedicated boots at farm entrances. Quarantine is critical for TR4 containment â restrict movement of suckers, soil, and plant material between farms and regions; source only certified tissue-culture plantlets from registered nurseries; and report suspected TR4 to national plant protection organisations immediately.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Scout fields weekly for weevil holes, leaf streaks, aphid colonies, and toppling.
  2. Use only certified disease-free tissue-culture plantlets or hot-water-treated pared suckers.
  3. Maintain 2â3 m spacing and remove old leaves to reduce humidity and disease pressure.
  4. Apply Beauveria or Metarhizium to corms and traps every 4â6 weeks.
  5. Rotate fungicides by mode of action; never exceed label rates or pre-harvest intervals.
  6. Disinfect all tools and boots between plants and between blocks.
  7. Rogue and destroy BBTV-infected mats immediately; do not replant from them.
  8. Restrict movement of suckers and soil; report suspected TR4 to authorities at once.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Plant Production and Protection Resources
  • IITA â Banana and Plantain Research
  • CABI Crop Protection Compendium
  • Plantwise Knowledge Bank (CABI)
  • Alliance Bioversity International & CIAT â Musa Resources

quiz.q: What is the most destructive insect pest of bananas in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Banana weevils (Cosmopolites sordidus) tunnel into corms, causing stunting and yield loss.

quiz.q: How can you detect banana weevils in your farm?
options: B) Cut a pseudostem piece and place on ground
quiz.explanation: Weevils hide inside cut pseudostem pieces within 24 hours.

quiz.q: Which nematode is common in Uganda, Kenya, and Tanzania?
quiz.explanation: Radopholus similis is the burrowing nematode prevalent in East Africa.

quiz.q: What is a recommended organic treatment for nematodes?
quiz.explanation: Poultry manure at 5 kg per mat suppresses nematode populations.

quiz.q: Which virus do aphids transmit to bananas?
quiz.explanation: Aphids transmit BBTV, which causes bunched leaves and no bunch.

quiz.q: What is a sign of Panama disease?
options: B) Yellowing of older leaves and splitting pseudostem
quiz.explanation: Panama disease causes yellowing and pseudostem splitting due to vascular blockage.

quiz.q: Which chemical is used to treat Panama disease?
quiz.explanation: There is no chemical cure for Panama disease; only resistant varieties and sanitation work.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for bananas to reduce Sigatoka?
quiz.explanation: 3 m x 3 m spacing improves airflow and reduces humidity, lowering Sigatoka spread.

quiz.q: How often should you apply mancozeb for Black Sigatoka?
quiz.explanation: Mancozeb is applied every 14 days to control Black Sigatoka.

quiz.q: Which variety is resistant to Sigatoka?
quiz.explanation: FHIA-25 is a resistant hybrid recommended for Sigatoka management.

quiz.q: What is a symptom of Banana Bunchy Top Virus?
options: B) Narrow, upright leaves bunched at top
quiz.explanation: BBTV causes new leaves to be narrow and bunched at the top.

quiz.q: How is BBTV transmitted?
quiz.explanation: The banana aphid (Pentalonia nigronervosa) transmits BBTV.

quiz.q: What should you do with a plant infected with BBTV?
quiz.explanation: There is no cure; uproot and burn infected plants to prevent spread.

quiz.q: Which tool disinfectant is recommended for banana farms?
quiz.explanation: 10% bleach (1 part bleach to 9 parts water) kills viruses and fungi on tools.

quiz.q: What is the first step in Integrated Pest Management (IPM)?
quiz.explanation: IPM starts with prevention, including certified disease-free plantlets.

quiz.q: How often should you monitor your banana farm for pests?
quiz.explanation: Weekly monitoring helps detect pests before they reach damaging levels.

quiz.q: What is an action threshold for aphids?
options: B) 5 or more aphids per plant
quiz.explanation: Treat when you find 5 or more aphids per plant to prevent virus transmission.

quiz.q: Which biological control agent attacks weevil larvae?
quiz.explanation: Steinernema carpocapsae is an entomopathogenic nematode that kills weevil larvae.

quiz.q: What is the recommended rate for neem oil spray against aphids?
quiz.explanation: Neem oil at 10 ml per litre with soap is effective against aphids.

quiz.q: Which chemical is used as a soil drench for weevils?
quiz.explanation: Imidacloprid 200 SL at 0.5 ml per litre is applied as a soil drench for weevils.

quiz.q: What is the pre-harvest interval for imidacloprid?
quiz.explanation: Wait 7 days after imidacloprid application before harvesting.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid spraying during flowering?
quiz.explanation: Spraying during flowering kills bees and other pollinators.

quiz.q: What is a key sanitation practice after pruning?
options: C) Wash tools with water only
D) Use same tool on all plants
quiz.explanation: Disinfecting tools with 10% bleach prevents disease spread.

quiz.q: How should you dispose of infected banana plants?
quiz.explanation: Burning or deep burial (1 m) prevents spread of pests and diseases.

quiz.q: What is hot water treatment for suckers?
quiz.explanation: Hot water at 52Â°C for 20 minutes kills nematodes and weevil eggs in suckers.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid moving soil from an infected field?
options: B) It may carry Panama disease
quiz.explanation: Soil can carry Fusarium spores that cause Panama disease.

quiz.q: What is a quarantine practice for banana farms?
options: A) Sell suckers from infected areas
B) Restrict visitors and mark boundaries
D) Plant new bananas immediately after uprooting
quiz.explanation: Quarantine involves restricting movement and marking infected areas.

quiz.q: How long should you leave a field fallow after removing Panama disease-infected plants?
quiz.explanation: Leave fallow for 3 months, then plant a non-host crop before replanting bananas.

quiz.q: Which crop can be used in rotation to reduce nematodes?
quiz.explanation: Maize is a non-host for banana nematodes and helps reduce populations.

quiz.q: What is the recommended rate for copper hydroxide in organic Sigatoka control?
quiz.explanation: Copper hydroxide at 2 kg per hectare every 10 days controls Sigatoka organically.
